question.text: A speculator sells Nifty futures at 22,500 expecting a market decline. The initial margin is Rs. 1,50,000 per lot (lot size = 25). If Nifty falls to 22,000, what is the return on margin invested?

explanation.text: The Logic: Step-by-step (workbook page 94 bearish short futures example): 1. Sell price = 22,500; Buy price to cover = 22,000 2. Profit per unit = 22,500 - 22,000 = 500 3. Total profit = 500 x 25 (lot size) = Rs. 12,500 4. Margin invested = Rs. 1,50,000 5. Return on margin = (12,500 / 1,50,000) x 100 = 8.33% The cash-market equivalent of this bearish view would be selling 25 shares worth 22,500 x 25 = Rs. 5,62,500 and buying them back lower at 22,000. The same Rs. 500-per-unit move would give a return of only 2.22% on the full notional value. Note that cash-market short selling is possible only if the trader already holds the shares (or can borrow them); futures avoid this constraint. The Trap: Students may compute return on the notional contract value (2.22%) instead of return on the margin invested, missing the leverage benefit of futures. Note: Futures leverage amplifies both gains and losses; return on margin can be significantly higher than the percentage change in the underlying.
